## **1\. Executive Summary and Project Vision**

### **1.1 Project Overview and Provenance Convention**

This document serves as a complete Technical Product Requirements Document (PRD) and engineering research reference for reproducing and demonstrating the core contributions of the IJCNN 2025 paper *"A Hybrid Neural Approach to Speaker Verification with an Improved Additive Angular Margin Loss"* by Jahangir Alam, Abderrahim Fathan, and Md Shahidul Alam of the Computer Research Institute of Montreal (https\://doi.org/10.1109/IJCNN64981.2025.11228198)1. To maintain rigorous academic transparency across all stages of implementation, every architectural specification, mathematical derivation, and design parameter is explicitly categorized using three provenance markers. Statements marked as **\[Paper Fact\]** represent direct architectural specifications, equations, hyperparameters, or experimental results stated in the attached IJCNN 2025 manuscript1. Statements marked as **\[External Source\]** represent missing mathematical definitions, companion algorithmic parameters, or benchmark baselines recovered from primary external literature—specifically the authors' companion publications on AdaptiveDrop (https\://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10888609/ and https\://neurips2024-enlsp.github.io/papers/paper\_57.pdf)2, CAMSAT (https\://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10389758/)5, and Local Statistics Pooling5, alongside foundational works including SKA-TDNN (https\://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01005)8, SKNet (https\://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06586)10, ECAPA-TDNN12, and VoicePrivacy Challenge LibriSpeech benchmarks (https\://www\.voiceprivacychallenge.org/attacker/docs/Attacker\_Challenge\_Eval\_Plan.pdf)13. Statements marked as **\[Engineering Recommendation\]** denote concrete engineering decisions, scaled-down hyperparameters, and fallback strategies tailored specifically for execution within the hardware limits of a single free Google Colab GPU (NVIDIA T4 with 16 GB VRAM) or an Apple MacBook Pro equipped with an M3 Pro SoC (18 GB to 36 GB unified memory).  
**\[Paper Fact\]** The target paper addresses text-independent Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) under both supervised and self-supervised learning regimes1. The authors propose three primary architectural and algorithmic innovations to extract speaker-discriminative utterance-level representations. First, they introduce the **SKA-HNN Backbone**, a 30.91-million-parameter hybrid neural network that couples a 2D-CNN front-end enhanced by frequency-wise (fwSKA) and channel-wise (cwSKA) Selective Kernel Attention with a cascaded frame-level processor consisting of a TDNN-LSTM hybrid module followed by a Fully-TDNN module1. Second, they formulate **Multi-Level Attentive Statistics Pooling (MLASP)**, an aggregation mechanism that applies Multi-Level Feature Combination (MLFC) across the outputs of the 2D-CNN, TDNN-LSTM, and Fully-TDNN stages (![][image1]), augments those frame representations with sliding-window local mean and standard deviation context (![][image2]), and computes channel-dependent attentive first- and second-order statistics before projecting the utterance vector into a 192-dimensional speaker embedding1. Third, they propose **Improved Additive Angular Margin Softmax (IAAMSoftmax)**, which integrates ArcFace (AAMSoftmax, scale ![][image3], margin ![][image4]) with AdaptiveDrop, a dynamic online label-noise cleansing cascade that rectifies suspicious speaker labels and filters out training samples whose cosine similarity with their class prototype falls below ![][image5] (![][image6]) after a 5-epoch warm-up phase1.

### **1.2 Operational Definition of "Implemented Successfully" for a Lab Course**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** Reproducing the exact full-scale training run reported in the paper—which trained a 30.91M-parameter model containing wide 2D convolutions and sequential LSTMs on 1,092,009 utterances from 5,994 speakers in the VoxCeleb2 development set1—requires approximately 350 to 500 GPU-hours on high-end data-center accelerators, placing a verbatim full-scale run outside the reach of a free Google Colab T4 session or an Apple M3 Pro laptop. Within a university Data Science laboratory course, "implemented successfully" is therefore defined as **faithful structural and algorithmic reproduction at a controlled compute scale**. Specifically, the engineering implementation must empirically validate three scientific hypotheses from the paper on a clean, speaker-disjoint subset of **LibriSpeech** (train-clean-100 for training; dev-clean, test-clean, and test-other for evaluation)14.  
The first hypothesis is **Architectural Validity**: the scaled-down SKA-HNN backbone (scaled proportionally from ![][image7] at 30.91M parameters to ![][image8] at ![][image9] parameters; runner-up scale ![][image10] at ![][image11] parameters) must execute end-to-end with exact proportional tensor transformations and outperform both a parameter-matched ECAPA-TDNN baseline and ablated variants lacking fwSKA/cwSKA, MLFC, or local statistics context1. The second hypothesis is **Noise-Robust Loss Validity**: while IAAMSoftmax yields only a minor gain over standard AAMSoftmax on clean supervised labels (mirroring the paper's ![][image12] EER shift on VoxCeleb1-O1), it must deliver a substantial, statistically significant EER reduction when trained on noisy pseudo-labels generated by unsupervised clustering or under controlled synthetic label corruption (![][image13] corrupted speaker labels)1. The third hypothesis is **Interactive Live Demonstration**: the trained model checkpoint must power a low-latency (\<500 ms inference) interactive Gradio web application capable of live microphone enrollment, cosine-similarity verification, Detection Error Tradeoff (DET) curve inspection, UMAP speaker-cluster projection, and fwSKA/cwSKA attention weight visualization.

## **2\. Deep Paper Analysis**

### **2.1 Component-by-Component Mathematical and Conceptual Breakdown**

**\[Paper Fact\]** The proposed hybrid speaker verification system integrates four sequential stages: a 2D-CNN front-end incorporating frequency-wise and channel-wise Selective Kernel Attention, a cascaded frame-level network combining a TDNN-LSTM module and a Fully-TDNN module with local statistics context, a Multi-Level Attentive Statistics Pooling (MLASP) aggregator, and a classification head trained with the IAAMSoftmax loss function1.  
![][image27]

#### **2.1.1 Selective Kernel Attention (SKNet Foundation: Split, Fuse, Select)**

**\[External Source\]** Selective Kernel Networks (SKNet), originally introduced for computer vision by Li et al. (CVPR 2019, https\://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06586 and https\://openaccess.thecvf.com/content\_CVPR\_2019/papers/Li\_Selective\_Kernel\_Networks\_CVPR\_2019\_paper.pdf)10 and adapted to speaker verification by Mun et al. (SKA-TDNN, IEEE SLT 2022/2023, https\://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01005)8, allow convolutional neurons to dynamically adjust their receptive field sizes in a data-driven manner depending on the temporal-spectral scale of the input speech stimulus, such as rapidly changing plosive consonants versus sustained vowel formants8. Given an intermediate 3D feature map ![][image28] (where ![][image29] denotes channels, ![][image30] denotes frequency bins, and ![][image31] denotes time frames), the SKA mechanism executes three sequential operations1.  
During the **Split** stage, the input tensor ![][image32] is processed in parallel by ![][image33] convolutional branches ![][image34] with distinct kernel sizes ![][image35]1. Each branch consists of a 2D convolution that preserves spatial dimensions via padding, followed by Batch Normalization (BN) and a ReLU activation ![][image36], yielding branch outputs ![][image37] for ![][image38]9. In both Li et al.10 and Mun et al.9, ![][image39] branches are employed with effective kernel sizes ![][image40] and ![][image41], where the ![][image41] receptive field is realized either as a direct ![][image41] convolution with padding 2 or as a computationally efficient ![][image40] dilated convolution with dilation rate 2 and padding 29. During the **Fuse** stage, multi-scale information from all ![][image33] branches is combined via element-wise summation prior to global context extraction1:   
$$U=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}{U}_{{k}_{i}}\in {R}^{C\times F\times T}$$  
Next, 2D Global Average Pooling (GAP) compresses ![][image42] into a 1D global descriptor vector ![][image43]9. A bottleneck transformation consisting of a Fully Connected (FC) layer ![][image44], Batch Normalization (BN), and ReLU activation ![][image36] squeezes ![][image43] by a reduction ratio ![][image45] into a compact guidance vector ![][image46]8:  
![][image47]  
Finally, during the **Select** stage, soft attention weights across the ![][image33] branches are computed from ![][image46] using branch-specific linear projection matrices ![][image48] and a softmax operator over the branch index ![][image38]9. The output feature map ![][image49] is obtained by a weighted summation over the ![][image33] branches such that the branch weights sum to unity at every coordinate9.

#### **2.1.2 Frequency-Wise SKA (fwSKA) vs. Channel-Wise SKA (cwSKA)**

**\[Paper Fact & External Source\]** While Alam et al.1 describe fwSKA and cwSKA qualitatively as applying Split, Fuse, and Select operations along the frequency and channel axes inside each 2D-CNN ResBlock, the exact mathematical formulations originate in Mun et al. (https\://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.01005, Section 2 and Section 3.1)8. In **Channel-Wise SKA (cwSKA)**, conventional SKA pools across the frequency-time plane (![][image50]) to compute a channel-wise global descriptor ![][image51]8: \$\$s\_{cw}(c) \= \\frac{1}{F \\times T} \\sum\_{f=1}^{F} \\sum\_{t=1}^{T} U(c, f, t), \\quad \\forall c \\in {1, \\dots, C}\$\$The bottleneck projection uses ![][image52] where ![][image53] (with reduction ratio ![][image54] in Mun et al.8) to produce ![][image55]8. For each branch ![][image38] and channel ![][image56], attention weights ![][image57] are computed using projection matrices ![][image58]8:  
$${a}_{{k}_{i}}(c)=\frac{\exp ({A}_{{k}_{i},c}{z}_{cw})}{\sum\limits_{l=1}^{N}\exp ({A}_{{k}_{l},c}{z}_{cw})},{V}_{cw}(c,f,t)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}{a}_{{k}_{i}}(c){U}_{{k}_{i}}(c,f,t)$$  
In contrast, **Frequency-Wise SKA (fwSKA)** addresses the physical property that speaker-discriminative vocal tract characteristics—such as fundamental frequency ![][image59] and formant distributions ![][image60]—are localized along the frequency axis, meaning channel-only recalibration misses frequency-domain non-stationarity8. Accordingly, fwSKA pools across the channel-time plane (![][image61]) to produce a frequency-wise descriptor ![][image62]8:\$\$s\_{fw}(f) \= \\frac{1}{C \\times T} \\sum\_{c=1}^{C} \\sum\_{t=1}^{T} U(c, f, t), \\quad \\forall f \\in {1, \\dots, F}\$\$A frequency bottleneck ![][image63] (with ![][image64], where for ![][image65] and ![][image54], ![][image66]) computes ![][image67]9. Branch projection matrices ![][image68] then yield frequency-bin attention weights across the ![][image33] branches8:  
![][image69]  
Inside each ResBlock of the 2D-CNN front-end (termed the fcwSKA block in Mun et al.9), an input tensor ![][image70] passes sequentially through a 2D convolution (Conv2d \+ BN \+ ReLU), fwSKA, cwSKA, and a 2D Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) layer before adding the residual skip connection ![][image71]1.

#### **2.1.4 Local Statistics (LS) Pooling**

**\[Paper Fact & External Source\]** A signature design element of Alam et al.'s architecture is the repeated extraction and concatenation of Local Statistics (LS) at three distinct locations: after the 2D-CNN (![][image80]), after the TDNN-LSTM (![][image81]), and inside the MLASP module (![][image82])1. The paper states that during local statistics pooling, 1st- and 2nd-order statistics are computed by resampling input sequences and adjusting pooling window shift rates to align with the frame-level features1, and later confirms that for ![][image83], local statistics pooling computes mean ![][image84] and standard deviation ![][image85], both matching the temporal length ![][image86] and feature dimension ![][image87]1. Drawing from the authors' prior formulation of Multi-Level Global-Local Statistics Pooling (Kang, Alam, and Fathan, IEEE ASRU 2021\)1, given a frame-level sequence ![][image88] and a local sliding window of odd length ![][image89] with symmetric boundary replication padding ![][image90], the local mean ![][image91] and local standard deviation ![][image92] around frame ![][image93] over the local neighborhood ![][image94] are defined as:

#### **2.1.5 Frame-Level Cascade: TDNN-LSTM Hybrid and Fully-TDNN Modules**

**\[Paper Fact\]** Rather than employing Res2Net blocks as in ECAPA-TDNN12 or multi-scale SKA blocks (msSKA) as in SKA-TDNN9, Alam et al. process the flattened 2D-CNN output ![][image103] through a two-stage cascade inspired by their earlier CNN-LSTM-TDNN hybrid architectures1. First, the **TDNN-LSTM Hybrid Module** takes ![][image104], applies a single 1D convolution layer (Conv1d \+ ReLU \+ BN) to capture short-term inter-frame context, and feeds the result into a single LSTM layer (LSTM \+ ReLU \+ BN) to model long-range sequential dependencies across the utterance, outputting ![][image105]1. Second, the **Fully-TDNN Module** takes ![][image106] and passes it through three sequential 1D convolution blocks (Conv1d \+ ReLU \+ BN), outputting ![][image107]1.

#### **2.1.6 Standard Attentive Statistics Pooling (ASP), MLFC, and MLASP**

**\[Paper Fact\]** Standard Attentive Statistics Pooling (Desplanques et al., Interspeech 202012) computes frame importance weights ![][image108] over frame representations ![][image109] using a two-layer tanh-activated bottleneck network (Equations 1 and 2 in the paper1):   
$${e}_{t}={v}^{T}\tanh (W{x}_{t}+b),{\alpha }_{t}=\frac{\exp ({e}_{t})}{\sum\limits_{\tau =1}^{T}\exp ({e}_{\tau })}$$  
In the proposed framework, **Multi-Level Feature Combination (MLFC)** first concatenates the outputs of all three major stages along the feature dimension to preserve complementary multi-resolution cues1:  
![][image110]  
Next, **Multi-Level Attentive Statistics Pooling (MLASP)** computes local statistics ![][image111] on ![][image82] and forms the context-augmented tensor ![][image112]1. The attention scoring network takes ![][image113] as input, projects it into a bottleneck dimension ![][image114] via ![][image115], and projects back to the original feature dimension ![][image116] via ![][image117] so that the resulting attention weights match the dimensionality of ![][image82]1:  
![][image118]  
The utterance-level vector ![][image119] is normalized via Batch Normalization (ASP \+ BN) and passed through two FC \+ BN layers (![][image120]) to yield the 192-dimensional speaker embedding ![][image121]1.

#### **2.1.7 Additive Angular Margin Softmax (AAMSoftmax / ArcFace)**

**\[Paper Fact & External Source\]** Formulated by Deng et al. (CVPR 2019 / TPAMI 2021, https\://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07698)1, AAMSoftmax enforces intra-class compactness and inter-class discrepancy on the unit hypersphere. Given the ![][image122]\-th speaker embedding ![][image123] with ground-truth speaker label ![][image124] and learnable class center weights ![][image125] for ![][image126], both ![][image127] and ![][image128] are ![][image129]\-normalized so that their inner product equals the cosine of the angle ![][image130] between them1:  
![][image131]  
In practical implementation, ![][image132] is expanded via the trigonometric identity ![][image133] with a monotonicity safeguard when ![][image134]3.

#### **2.1.8 AdaptiveDrop and IAAMSoftmax**

**\[Paper Fact & External Source\]** When training on pseudo-labels generated by unsupervised clustering (or web-scraped datasets containing annotation errors), deep networks initially fit clean, dominant patterns during the first few epochs before gradually memorizing noisy labels—a phenomenon that inflates the cosine similarity of mislabeled samples toward wrong class centers and degrades verification generalization3. To prevent this memorization, Alam et al. integrate AdaptiveDrop (Fathan, Zhu, and Alam, ICASSP 2025 / ENLSP 2024 / Fathan PhD Thesis 2025, https\://spectrum.library.concordia.ca/id/eprint/995416/1/Fathan\_PhD\_W2025.pdf)2 into AAMSoftmax to form IAAMSoftmax (Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 of the paper1).  
At each training step, for each sample ![][image135] in mini-batch ![][image32] with current (potentially noisy) label ![][image136], the network extracts the ![][image129]\-normalized embedding ![][image137] on the fly and computes its cosine similarity against all learnable class centers ![][image138] for ![][image139]1:  
![][image140]  
During the initial warm-up phase (![][image141], with ![][image142] in the paper1), all samples in the mini-batch are retained without modification so that the class prototypes ![][image143] converge toward the dominant clean modes of each speaker cluster1. Once the epoch counter exceeds the Epoch to Start Correcting (ESC), **Stage 1 (Label Correction)** rectifies suspicious labels *before* sample filtering so that mislabeled samples belonging to another known speaker in the training set are reassigned rather than discarded, thereby mitigating over-cleaning1. Specifically, if a sample's similarity to its assigned label ![][image144] is below ![][image145], its rectified label ![][image146] is updated to the closest class prototype ![][image147] provided ![][image148]1. Once the epoch counter exceeds the Epoch to Start Dropping (ESD), **Stage 2 (Sample Filtering)** evaluates whether each sample's cosine similarity to its (possibly rectified) class prototype ![][image146] meets the cosine similarity threshold ![][image5] (![][image149])1:  
![][image150]  
The AAMSoftmax loss and subsequent backpropagation update are then computed exclusively over the retained clean subset ![][image151]1.

#### **2.1.9 CAMSAT Unsupervised Clustering**

**\[Paper Fact & External Source\]** In Section III and Section V, the authors evaluate self-supervised speaker verification by treating VoxCeleb2 dev as unlabeled, extracting 400-dimensional i-vectors4 from MFCC features, and clustering all 1,092,009 utterances into ![][image152] pseudo-speaker clusters using CAMSAT (*Augmentation Mix and Self-Augmented Training Clustering*, Fathan and Alam, IEEE ASRU 2023, https\://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10389758/)1. Building upon Information Maximizing Self-Augmented Training (IMSAT), CAMSAT trains a deep clustering classifier ![][image153] on the 400-dim i-vectors by simultaneously maximizing the mutual information ![][image154] between input representations and cluster assignments (encouraging balanced cluster sizes via marginal entropy ![][image155] and confident one-hot assignments via conditional entropy ![][image156]) while enforcing prediction invariance between original i-vectors and augmentation-mixed / latent-perturbed counterparts via Kullback-Leibler divergence5.

### **2.4 Critical Assessment: Novelty, Ablation Validity, and Architectural Weaknesses**

**\[Engineering Analysis\]** A rigorous architectural critique reveals how the components of the IJCNN 2025 paper interact and where its primary scientific and empirical contributions lie. Each individual building block in the paper was previously introduced either by Mun et al. (fcwSKA 2D-CNN front-end in SKA-TDNN, SLT 20229) or by the CRIM authors themselves in separate conference venues—specifically CNN-LSTM-TDNN hybrids in SPECOM 20211, Local Statistics Pooling in ASRU 20217, Cross/Self-Module Attentive Statistics Pooling in IJCB 20231, CAMSAT clustering in ASRU 20236, and AdaptiveDrop in ENLSP 2024 and ICASSP 20252. The genuine contribution of the IJCNN 2025 manuscript is its **system-level synthesis**: replacing the Res2Net/msSKA 1D backbone of SKA-TDNN with a local-statistics-augmented TDNN-LSTM and Fully-TDNN cascade, and coupling that hybrid extractor with AdaptiveDrop inside IAAMSoftmax1.  
![][image270]  
A deeper inspection of the parameter distribution in Section 2.2 exposes an important structural inefficiency in the authors' design. In SKA-TDNN (Mun et al.9), the final 2D-CNN layer reduces the channel count to 64 and downsamples the temporal dimension by a factor of 2 (![][image271]), keeping total model parameters at ![][image272]9. In contrast, Alam et al. keep ![][image158] and preserve full temporal resolution ![][image86], producing ![][image103] and then tripling its channel dimension via Local Statistics to ![][image273]1. Consequently, the single Conv1d(7680, 512, k=3) transition layer inside TDNN-LSTM consumes **11.80M parameters** (38.2% of the entire network), and the MLASP projection consumes another **8.81M parameters** because ![][image80] (![][image221]\-dim) dominates ![][image82] (![][image274]\-dim)1.  
Evaluating the ablations in Table II (![][image21] through ![][image22]) confirms that the progression from ![][image22] (![][image275] EER, no 2D-CNN) to ![][image276] (![][image277] EER, vanilla 2D-CNN) and ![][image226] (![][image278] EER, SKA 2D-CNN) persuasively demonstrates that 2D time-frequency convolutions with frequency-channel attention (fwSKA \+ cwSKA) substantially outperform 1D TDNNs alone1. Similarly, the improvement from ![][image279] (![][image280] EER) to ![][image226] (![][image278] EER) proves that concatenating multi-level representations (![][image281]) prevents information loss across the sequential LSTM bottleneck1. However, two methodological weaknesses must be noted when presenting this paper to examiners. First, the ablation in Table II does not control for parameter count, comparing ![][image22] at 6.34M parameters directly against ![][image226] at 30.91M parameters1. Second, in the supervised regime (Table IV), IAAMSoftmax improves EER over standard AAMSoftmax by only ![][image282] on VoxCeleb1-O (![][image12]), ![][image283] on VoxCeleb1-E (![][image284]), and ![][image283] on VoxCeleb1-H (![][image285])1—a difference small enough to fall within single-seed training variance. The true empirical justification for IAAMSoftmax only emerges in **Section V (Table VI)** under self-supervised clustering noise, where it reduces EER from ![][image286] to ![][image287] (![][image288] relative reduction)1. Consequently, **including Tier 3 (noisy labels and clustering pseudo-labels) in the student project is indispensable to demonstrate the mechanism for which IAAMSoftmax was designed**.

### **3.2 Confirming LibriSpeech Over LibriTTS**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** The initial inclination toward **LibriSpeech** (http\://www\.openslr.org/12)14 over **LibriTTS** (http\://www\.openslr.org/60)14 is **strongly confirmed** by three concrete signal-processing and experimental factors. First, the target paper extracts 80-dimensional Mel-filterbank (MFB) features using a 25 ms analysis window (400 samples at 16 kHz) and a 10 ms frame shift (160 samples at 16 kHz) spanning up to an 8 kHz Nyquist frequency1. LibriSpeech is natively sampled at 16 kHz FLAC14, whereas LibriTTS is sampled at 24 kHz WAV14; using LibriTTS either requires on-the-fly Kaiser-window resampling (which adds a 15% to 25% CPU data-loading bottleneck) or alters the frequency bin spacing of the 80 Mel filters, distorting the frequency axis over which fwSKA learns its attention weights. Second, in constructing LibriTTS specifically for text-to-speech synthesis, Zen et al. (2019) split audio at sentence boundaries, stripped internal pauses, and rejected utterances with background noise or book-chapter acoustic variations14. Consequently, LibriTTS train-clean-100 retains only 53.8 hours of speech (compared to 100.6 hours in LibriSpeech train-clean-100) and eliminates the natural intra-speaker acoustic variability needed to train a discriminative speaker verification backbone. Third, the **VoicePrivacy Challenge (2020, 2022, 2024\)** uses LibriSpeech (train-clean-360 for ASV training; dev-clean and test-clean for ASV evaluation with ECAPA-TDNN and x-vector extractors) as an official, peer-reviewed speaker verification benchmark (https\://www\.voiceprivacychallenge.org/vp2020/docs/VoicePrivacy\_2022\_Eval\_Plan\_v1.0.pdf)13, providing direct literature baselines to cite in the lab report and viva.

### **3.3 Recommended Primary and Stretch Dataset Plan**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** The **Primary Dataset Plan** uses a multi-condition, strictly speaker-disjoint split of **LibriSpeech** (http\://www\.openslr.org/12)14. For training, the default partition is train-clean-100, which comprises **251 speakers** (125 female and 126 male), **28,539 utterances**, and **100.6 hours** of 16 kHz speech in a **6.3 GB** archive14 (with train-clean-360 at 921 speakers and 23 GB serving as the runner-up if extra storage is available15). Training on 28,539 utterances at a batch size of 64 yields 446 gradient updates per epoch; on a Colab T4 or Mac M3 Pro with mixed precision (fp16), one epoch of the scaled SKA-HNN completes in **\~55 seconds**, allowing a full 30-epoch training run to finish in **\~28 minutes**. For validation, the pipeline uses dev-clean (**40 speakers**, 2,703 utterances, 5.4 hours, 337 MB)14 exclusively for learning-rate monitoring, early stopping, and calibrating the decision threshold ![][image289]. For final evaluation, the pipeline uses two speaker-disjoint partitions representing distinct acoustic difficulty levels: test-clean (**40 speakers**, 2,620 utterances, 5.4 hours, 346 MB)14, which serves as the matched clean condition analogous to VoxCeleb1-O, and test-other (**33 speakers**, 2,939 utterances, 5.3 hours, 328 MB)13, which contains speakers with stronger accents, prosodic variations, or lower recording SNR and serves as a challenging domain-mismatch condition analogous to VoxCeleb1-H. In LibriSpeech, speaker IDs are globally unique integers encoded as the top-level directory and first hyphen-delimited field of every filename (\<speaker\_id\>-\<chapter\_id\>-\<utterance\_id\>.flac), guaranteeing that the intersection of speaker IDs across train-clean-100, dev-clean, test-clean, and test-other is strictly the empty set (![][image290])14.  
For the **Optional Stretch Dataset Plan (Tier 4\)**, the recommended default is **Zero-Shot Cross-Dataset Evaluation on Official VoxCeleb1-O** (**40 speakers**, **4,874 WAV files**, **\~1.2 GB**, 37,720 official trials1), which can be downloaded standalone from HuggingFace (https\://huggingface.co/datasets/ProgramComputer/voxceleb) to evaluate the LibriSpeech-trained SKA-HNN alongside a pretrained SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN directly on the paper's exact Table I / Table IV benchmark1. The runner-up stretch dataset is **CN-Celeb1** (http\://www\.openslr.org/82, 9.2 GB, 1,000 speakers across 11 genres), which the authors explicitly cite in Section IV-B3 (Ref \[52\]) to demonstrate multi-genre generalization1.

### **3.4 Verification Trial-List Generation Algorithm**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** Because LibriSpeech filenames follow the hierarchy \<speaker\_id\>-\<chapter\_id\>-\<utterance\_id\>.flac, each \<chapter\_id\> corresponds to a distinct audiobook chapter recording session, often captured on different days with slightly different microphone proximity and room tone. If target trials are drawn from the *same* \<chapter\_id\>, a neural network can artificially inflate accuracy by matching stationary background room acoustics rather than vocal tract biometrics. Therefore, the custom trial generator **must enforce cross-session (different \<chapter\_id\>) target pairs whenever a speaker has ![][image291] recorded chapters**, and **gender-matched impostor pairs** for negative trials (replicating the VoxCeleb1-H hard protocol1). Each generated trial file is formatted as \<label\> \<utt\_path\_1\> \<utt\_path\_2\> with \<label\> \\in \\{1, 0\\}\$19, using a deterministic random seed (seed=42\`) and excluding fragments shorter than ![][image292]:

> * trials\_dev\_clean.txt: **20,000 trials** (10,000 cross-chapter target trials and 10,000 gender-matched non-target trials across the 40 speakers of dev-clean).  
> * trials\_test\_clean.txt (**Standard Clean Condition**, analogous to VoxCeleb1-O): **30,000 trials** (15,000 cross-chapter target trials and 15,000 gender-matched non-target trials across the 40 speakers of test-clean).  
> * trials\_test\_other\_hard.txt (**Hard Mismatched Condition**, analogous to VoxCeleb1-H): **30,000 trials** (15,000 cross-chapter target trials and 15,000 gender-matched non-target trials across the 33 speakers of test-other).

### **3.5 Augmentation Resources (MUSAN and RIRS\_NOISES) and Lightweight Fallbacks**

**\[Paper Fact & Engineering Recommendation\]** The paper applies on-the-fly acoustic augmentation using MUSAN noise, speed perturbation with rates between ![][image293] and ![][image294], reverberation (RIR), and SpecAugment time-frequency masking1. While RIRS\_NOISES (http\://www\.openslr.org/28, 1.3 GB zip) is compact enough to download directly in any Colab or local session, the full MUSAN corpus (http\://www\.openslr.org/17, 11 GB tar.gz) can strain free Colab disk quotas. Therefore, the **recommended default** is to download RIRS\_NOISES (1.3 GB) for authentic room reverberation (torchaudio.functional.fftconvolve), apply native torchaudio speed perturbation (factors=\[0.95, 1.0, 1.05\]) and SpecAugment (FrequencyMasking(10) and TimeMasking(15))1, and replace the 11 GB MUSAN archive with a **zero-download on-the-fly noise synthesizer** that mixes (a) multi-speaker **in-batch babble noise** (summing 3 to 5 randomly selected background utterances from other speakers in the training manifest at ![][image295]) and (b) synthetic Gaussian white and pink noise at ![][image296]. The runner-up option, when running locally on the Mac M3 Pro with ample SSD space, is to download the full 11 GB MUSAN archive from OpenSLR.

### **3.6 Expected Achievable EER Range and Explaining the Gap to Examiners**

**\[External Source & Engineering Estimate\]** Published literature provides a firm anchor for expected EER on LibriSpeech. In the VoicePrivacy Challenge 2022/2024 Evaluation Plans and Franzreb et al. (ISCA SPSC 2025, https\://www\.isca-archive.org/spsc\_2025/franzreb25\_spsc.pdf)13, an ECAPA-TDNN (![][image297]) or Kaldi x-vector trained on train-clean-360 (921 speakers) achieves an unprotected single-enrollment EER of ![][image298] on test-clean13. Furthermore, empirical scaling analysis on LibriSpeech (https\://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10665418/)20 demonstrates that speaker verification EER decays logarithmically with the number of training speakers ![][image299] according to the regression ![][image300], reporting ![][image301] **EER** on LibriSpeech test-clean under smaller speaker setups and dropping from ![][image302] (![][image303]) to ![][image304] (![][image305]) and ![][image306] (![][image307])20.  
Based on this logarithmic scaling law and our compute budget (training on train-clean-100 with ![][image308] speakers for 30 epochs), the **estimated achievable EER range** is ![][image309] on test-clean (![][image310] on test-other) for the Tier 0 ECAPA-TDNN baseline, improving to ![][image311] on test-clean (![][image312] on test-other) for the Tier 1 scaled SKA-HNN (![][image8]). When explaining the numerical gap between ![][image313] EER on LibriSpeech and the paper's ![][image16] EER on VoxCeleb1-O1 to examiners, three quantitative points provide a complete defense:

> 1. **Speaker Diversity Ratio (![][image314] fewer training speakers)**: Deep angular metric learning (AAMSoftmax) constructs a discriminative hyperspherical basis spanned by the training speaker prototypes ![][image315]. The paper trains on ![][image316] speakers (1,092,009 utterances) in VoxCeleb2 dev1, whereas train-clean-100 provides ![][image317] speakers (28,539 utterances). Substituting ![][image318] vs. ![][image308] into the empirical relation ![][image319]20 directly accounts for the shift in absolute EER.  
> 2. **Channel Width Scaling (![][image320] fewer parameters)**: Scaling ![][image321] and ![][image322] reduces parameter count from ![][image227] to ![][image323] so that training fits within student GPU constraints and avoids severe overfitting on 251 speakers.  
> 3. **Relative Ranking Invariance**: Scientific validation of the paper depends not on matching the absolute ![][image16] VoxCeleb2 figure, but on reproducing the **exact relative ordering of systems**: SKA-HNN (![][image324]) \< ECAPA-TDNN \< SKA-HNN withoutLS context (![][image228]) \< SKA-HNN without MLFC (![][image279]) \< SKA-HNN with vanilla 2D-CNN (![][image276]) \< SKA-HNN without 2D-CNN (![][image22]), alongside IAAMSoftmax \< AAMSoftmax under noisy labels1.

## **4\. Scoped Project Plan with Tiers**

**\[Paper Fact & Engineering Analysis\]** While IAAMSoftmax yields only a marginal ![][image282] EER reduction in fully supervised training on clean labels (Table IV), its primary algorithmic purpose is demonstrated in Section V (Tables VI and VII), where it combats the heavy label noise inherent in clustering-generated pseudo-labels (![][image25] EER, outperforming all 12 self-supervised baselines)1.

## **5\. System Architecture and Technical Design**

### **5.1 End-to-End Pipeline Architecture Description**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** The software system is architected as a modular, configuration-driven PyTorch pipeline comprising ten decoupled functional stages. In the first stage (**Data Preparation and Manifest Builder**, src/data/prep\_librispeech.py), the system scans raw LibriSpeech directories (train-clean-100, dev-clean, test-clean, test-other), extracts speaker ID, chapter ID, and audio duration via torchaudio.info, builds contiguous speaker-to-integer label mappings (0 to 250), and writes deterministic CSV manifests alongside SHA-256 verified verification trial lists. In the second stage (**Audio Loader and Waveform Augmentation**, src/data/dataset.py), the training dataset loader crops a random 180-frame segment (![][image341] samples ![][image342] at 16 kHz)1, applies on-the-fly waveform augmentations (speed perturbation ![][image343], additive noise/babble, or RIR convolution)1, and normalizes utterance amplitude. In the third stage (**Acoustic Feature Extraction and SpecAugment**, src/features/mfb.py), the pipeline computes 80-dimensional log Mel-filterbank energies (![][image344], window=400, hop=160, Hamming window), applies instance-level cepstral mean normalization (CMN) across time, and applies on-the-fly SpecAugment (frequency masking up to 10 bins, time masking up to 15 frames) during training1.  
In the fourth stage (**SKA-HNN Backbone**, src/models/ska\_hnn.py), the ![][image161] acoustic tensor passes through the 2D-CNN \+ fwSKA/cwSKA front-end (![][image80]), LocalStatsPool1d \+ TDNN-LSTM (![][image81]), LocalStatsPool1d \+ Fully-TDNN (![][image223]), MLFC concatenation (![][image345]), MLASP with local statistics context (![][image346]), and the FC+BN embedding projection to yield ![][image347]1. In the fifth stage (**IAAMSoftmax Objective with Online AdaptiveDrop**, src/losses/iaam\_softmax.py), the loss module maintains ![][image129]\-normalized class prototypes ![][image348] and, conditioned on the current epoch relative to ESC and ESD, performs online label correction and cosine-threshold sample filtering (![][image5]) before computing the angular margin cross-entropy loss (![][image326])1. In the sixth stage (**Training Engine**, src/engine/trainer.py), the trainer coordinates mixed-precision (torch.amp.autocast), gradient clipping (max\_norm=3.0), CyclicLR scheduling, linear margin warm-up, TensorBoard logging of AdaptiveDrop retention rates, and top\-![][image349] checkpoint persistence based on validation EER. In the seventh stage (**Full-Utterance Embedding Extractor**, src/engine/extractor.py), the evaluator extracts ![][image129]\-normalized 192-dimensional embeddings over full-duration evaluation utterances and caches them in memory keyed by utterance ID. In the eighth stage (**Cosine Scoring and AS-Norm**, src/eval/scorer.py), the backend computes inner products between ![][image129]\-normalized enrollment and test embeddings for every pair in the trial list1. In the ninth stage (**Biometric Evaluator**, src/eval/metrics.py), the system computes Equal Error Rate (EER), minDCF (![][image350])17, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, DET curves, and target/impostor score histograms. Finally, in the tenth stage (**Interactive Demonstration App**, app/gradio\_demo.py), a 5-tab Gradio interface exposes live microphone/file enrollment, impostor verification, DET/histogram inspection, UMAP speaker clusters, and fwSKA/cwSKA attention weight heatmaps.

### **5.2 Repository Structure and Configuration Management**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** All source files, YAML configurations, unit tests, and demo assets are organized into a modular directory structure governed by OmegaConf YAML files so that switching between Tier 0, Tier 1, Tier 2 ablations (![][image24]), and Tier 3 noisy-label experiments requires only a command-line flag.

| Directory / File Path | Architectural Responsibility & Contents |
| :---- | :---- |
| configs/\*.yaml | Experiment configurations: default.yaml, tier0\_ecapa.yaml, tier1\_ska\_hnn.yaml, tier2\_ablations.yaml, tier3\_noisy\_ssl.yaml. |
| data/manifests/ | Generated CSV manifests (train\_clean\_100.csv, dev\_clean.csv, test\_clean.csv, test\_other.csv), trial lists (trials\_\*.txt), and checksums.sha256. |
| src/data/ | download.py, prep\_librispeech.py, trial\_generator.py (cross-chapter/gender-matched builder), dataset.py (180-frame cropper), augment.py (RIR, babble, speed). |
| src/models/ | ska\_modules.py (FrequencyWiseSKA, ChannelWiseSKA, SEBlock2D, SKAResBlock), pooling.py (LocalStatsPool1d, MLASP), ska\_hnn.py (SKAHNN), ecapa\_baseline.py. |
| src/losses/ | iaam\_softmax.py (IAAMSoftmax with AdaptiveDrop label correction, cosine threshold filtering, and margin scheduling). |
| src/ssl/ | clustering.py (MFCC/bootstrap embedding extraction, KMeans/AgglomerativeClustering pseudo-labeler, and controlled synthetic label-noise injector). |
| src/engine/ & src/utils/ | trainer.py, evaluator.py, metrics.py (compute\_eer\_and\_mindcf, bootstrap\_ci), plots.py (DET, histograms, UMAP, SKA heatmaps), seed.py. |
| app/ | gradio\_demo.py (5-tab interactive UI) and app/demo\_assets/ (pre-recorded enrollment and impostor WAV files for offline viva fallback). |
| scripts/ & tests/ | CLI entrypoints (train.py, evaluate.py, run\_ablations.py, run\_ssl\_noise.py) and pytest suite (test\_shapes.py, test\_metrics.py, test\_loss.py). |

### **5.3 PyTorch Implementation Skeletons (Write Yourself vs. Borrow)**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** To uphold strict academic integrity in a university course while maximizing engineering velocity, the table below delineates which components must be implemented from scratch ("Write Yourself" — the core contributions of Alam et al.1) and which standard utilities can be adapted or borrowed with attribution.

| Component | Implementation Status | Source / Attribution Strategy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| fwSKA, cwSKA, and SKAResBlock | **MUST WRITE YOURSELF** | Core paper front-end1 based on equations in Mun et al. (https\://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01005)9. |
| LocalStatsPool1d & MLASP | **MUST WRITE YOURSELF** | Core paper pooling contribution1 (sliding window mean/std \+ context-augmented attention). |
| TDNN-LSTM, Fully-TDNN, & SKAHNN Router | **MUST WRITE YOURSELF** | Core paper cascade & ablation switches (![][image21] through ![][image22])1. |
| IAAMSoftmax & AdaptiveDrop | **MUST WRITE YOURSELF** | Core paper loss contribution (Algorithm 1: online label correction \+ ![][image5] filtering)1. |
| LibriSpeech Trial-List Builder | **MUST WRITE YOURSELF** | Custom cross-chapter target / gender-matched impostor generator for LibriSpeech. |
| ECAPA-TDNN Baseline (Tier 0\) | **BORROW / ADAPT WITH ATTRIBUTION** | Use speechbrain.lobes.models.ECAPA\_TDNN17 or adapt TaoRuijie's ECAPA-TDNN (MIT License). |
| Audio Feature Extraction (MelSpectrogram, SpecAugment) | **BORROW STANDARD LIBRARY** | Use torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram, FrequencyMasking, TimeMasking. |

#### **5.3.1 PyTorch Code: fwSKA, cwSKA, SE2d, and SKAResBlock (Write Yourself)**

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn  
import torch.nn.functional as F

class FrequencyWiseSKA(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Frequency-wise Selective Kernel Attention (fwSKA).  
    Pools across (Channel, Time) to recalibrate multi-scale kernel branches along Frequency (F).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, channels: int, freq\_bins: int, reduction: int \= 8):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.channels \= channels  
        self.freq\_bins \= freq\_bins  
        d\_f \= max(freq\_bins // reduction, 4\)

        \# Split: N=2 branches with 3x3 (d=1) and effective 5x5 (k=3, d=2) receptive fields  
        self.branch1 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, dilation=1, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )  
        self.branch2 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=1, padding=2, dilation=2, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )

        \# Fuse: Squeeze frequency descriptor s\_fw of shape (B, F) \-\> z\_fw of shape (B, d\_f)  
        self.fc\_squeeze \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(freq\_bins, d\_f, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(d\_f),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )  
        \# Select: Project z\_fw \-\> 2 branches of shape (B, 2, F)  
        self.fc\_select \= nn.Linear(d\_f, 2 \* freq\_bins)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, return\_attn: bool \= False):  
        \# x: (B, C, F, T)  
        B, C, F\_bins, T \= x.shape  
        u1 \= self.branch1(x)  \# (B, C, F, T)  
        u2 \= self.branch2(x)  \# (B, C, F, T)  
        u\_sum \= u1 \+ u2       \# Fuse element-wise

        \# Global Average Pooling across C and T \-\> s\_fw: (B, F)  
        s\_fw \= u\_sum.mean(dim=(1, 3))  
        z\_fw \= self.fc\_squeeze(s\_fw)  \# (B, d\_f)

        \# Compute branch attention weights across frequency bins  
        logits \= self.fc\_select(z\_fw).view(B, 2, F\_bins)  \# (B, 2, F)  
        attn \= F.softmax(logits, dim=1)                   \# (B, 2, F)

        a1 \= attn\[:, 0, :\].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(-1)     \# (B, 1, F, 1\)  
        a2 \= attn\[:, 1, :\].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(-1)     \# (B, 1, F, 1\)  
        out \= a1 \* u1 \+ a2 \* u2                           \# (B, C, F, T)  
        if return\_attn:  
            return out, attn  
        return out

class ChannelWiseSKA(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Channel-wise Selective Kernel Attention (cwSKA).  
    Pools across (Frequency, Time) to recalibrate multi-scale kernel branches along Channel (C).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, channels: int, reduction: int \= 8):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        d\_c \= max(channels // reduction, 8\)

        self.branch1 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, dilation=1, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )  
        self.branch2 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=1, padding=2, dilation=2, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )

        self.fc\_squeeze \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(channels, d\_c, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(d\_c),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )  
        self.fc\_select \= nn.Linear(d\_c, 2 \* channels)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, return\_attn: bool \= False):  
        \# x: (B, C, F, T)  
        B, C, F\_bins, T \= x.shape  
        u1 \= self.branch1(x)  
        u2 \= self.branch2(x)  
        u\_sum \= u1 \+ u2

        \# Global Average Pooling across F and T \-\> s\_cw: (B, C)  
        s\_cw \= u\_sum.mean(dim=(2, 3))  
        z\_cw \= self.fc\_squeeze(s\_cw)                      \# (B, d\_c)

        logits \= self.fc\_select(z\_cw).view(B, 2, C)       \# (B, 2, C)  
        attn \= F.softmax(logits, dim=1)                   \# (B, 2, C)

        a1 \= attn\[:, 0, :\].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)    \# (B, C, 1, 1\)  
        a2 \= attn\[:, 1, :\].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1)    \# (B, C, 1, 1\)  
        out \= a1 \* u1 \+ a2 \* u2  
        if return\_attn:  
            return out, attn  
        return out

class SEBlock2D(nn.Module):  
    """2D Squeeze-and-Excitation layer operating on channel axis."""  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, channels: int, reduction: int \= 8):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        mid \= max(channels // reduction, 8\)  
        self.se \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(channels, mid, bias=False),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),  
            nn.Linear(mid, channels, bias=False),  
            nn.Sigmoid()  
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        B, C, \_, \_ \= x.shape  
        s \= x.mean(dim=(2, 3))                            \# (B, C)  
        g \= self.se(s).view(B, C, 1, 1\)                   \# (B, C, 1, 1\)  
        return x \* g

class SKAResBlock(nn.Module):  
    """  
    ResBlock in 2D-CNN Front-End: Conv2d \-\> fwSKA \-\> cwSKA \-\> SE \-\> Residual Skip.  
    Supports ablation S5 (use\_ska=False replaces fwSKA+cwSKA with standard Conv2d).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, channels: int, freq\_bins: int, reduction: int \= 8, use\_ska: bool \= True):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.use\_ska \= use\_ska  
        self.conv1 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        )  
        if use\_ska:  
            self.fw\_ska \= FrequencyWiseSKA(channels, freq\_bins, reduction)  
            self.cw\_ska \= ChannelWiseSKA(channels, reduction)  
        else:  
            \# S5 Ablation: Vanilla 2D-CNN ResBlock without SKA  
            self.vanilla\_conv \= nn.Sequential(  
                nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel\_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False),  
                nn.BatchNorm2d(channels),  
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
            )  
        self.se \= SEBlock2D(channels, reduction)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        residual \= x  
        out \= self.conv1(x)  
        if self.use\_ska:  
            out \= self.fw\_ska(out)  
            out \= self.cw\_ska(out)  
        else:  
            out \= self.vanilla\_conv(out)  
        out \= self.se(out)  
        return F.relu(out \+ residual, inplace=True)

#### **5.3.2 PyTorch Code: LocalStatsPool1d, TDNNLSTMModule, FullyTDNNModule, MLASP, and Full SKAHNN**

Python  
class LocalStatsPool1d(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Computes sliding-window 1st-order (mean) and 2nd-order (std) local statistics  
    aligned to the exact frame length T.  
    Input: (B, D, T) \-\> Output: (B, 2\*D, T)  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, window\_size: int \= 21, eps: float \= 1e-5):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        assert window\_size % 2 \== 1, "window\_size must be odd to preserve frame length T"  
        self.window\_size \= window\_size  
        self.pad \= window\_size // 2  
        self.eps \= eps

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        \# x: (B, D, T)  
        x\_pad \= F.pad(x, (self.pad, self.pad), mode="replicate")  
        local\_mean \= F.avg\_pool1d(x\_pad, kernel\_size=self.window\_size, stride=1)  
        local\_sq\_mean \= F.avg\_pool1d(x\_pad \* x\_pad, kernel\_size=self.window\_size, stride=1)  
        local\_var \= torch.clamp(local\_sq\_mean \- local\_mean \* local\_mean, min=self.eps)  
        local\_std \= torch.sqrt(local\_var)  
        return torch.cat(\[local\_mean, local\_std\], dim=1)  \# (B, 2\*D, T)

class Conv1dReLUBN(nn.Module):  
    """Standard 1D TDNN block: Conv1d \+ ReLU \+ BatchNorm1d."""  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_ch: int, out\_ch: int, kernel\_size: int \= 3, dilation: int \= 1):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        padding \= dilation \* (kernel\_size \- 1\) // 2  
        self.net \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv1d(in\_ch, out\_ch, kernel\_size=kernel\_size, stride=1,  
                      padding=padding, dilation=dilation, bias=False),  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(out\_ch)  
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        return self.net(x)

class TDNNLSTMModule(nn.Module):  
    """  
    TDNN-LSTM Hybrid Module (Blue rectangle in Figure 1).  
    Input: \[X\_c; LS(X\_c)\] of shape (B, 3\*d\_c, T) \-\> Output: X\_l of shape (B, C1, T)  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_dim: int, out\_dim: int \= 256):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.tdnn \= Conv1dReLUBN(in\_dim, out\_dim, kernel\_size=3, dilation=1)  
        self.lstm \= nn.LSTM(input\_size=out\_dim, hidden\_size=out\_dim,  
                            num\_layers=1, batch\_first=True, bidirectional=False)  
        self.relu \= nn.ReLU(inplace=True)  
        self.bn \= nn.BatchNorm1d(out\_dim)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        \# x: (B, 3\*d\_c, T)  
        h \= self.tdnn(x)                     \# (B, C1, T)  
        h\_seq \= h.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()  \# (B, T, C1)  
        lstm\_out, \_ \= self.lstm(h\_seq)       \# (B, T, C1)  
        lstm\_out \= lstm\_out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()  \# (B, C1, T)  
        return self.bn(self.relu(lstm\_out))

class FullyTDNNModule(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Fully-TDNN Module (Green rectangle in Figure 1): 3 cascaded Conv1d+ReLU+BN layers.  
    Input: \[X\_l; LS(X\_l)\] of shape (B, 3\*C1, T) \-\> Output: X\_t of shape (B, C1, T)  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_dim: int, out\_dim: int \= 256):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.net \= nn.Sequential(  
            Conv1dReLUBN(in\_dim, out\_dim, kernel\_size=3, dilation=1),  
            Conv1dReLUBN(out\_dim, out\_dim, kernel\_size=3, dilation=2),  
            Conv1dReLUBN(out\_dim, out\_dim, kernel\_size=3, dilation=3),  
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        return self.net(x)

class MLASP(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Multi-Level Attentive Statistics Pooling (MLASP) with optional Local Statistics Context.  
    Supports S2/S4 ablation (use\_ls\_context=False).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, feat\_dim: int, attn\_dim: int \= 128,  
                 use\_ls\_context: bool \= True, window\_size: int \= 21, eps: float \= 1e-5):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.feat\_dim \= feat\_dim  
        self.use\_ls\_context \= use\_ls\_context  
        self.eps \= eps

        if use\_ls\_context:  
            self.ls\_pool \= LocalStatsPool1d(window\_size=window\_size, eps=eps)  
            in\_attn\_dim \= 3 \* feat\_dim  
        else:  
            in\_attn\_dim \= feat\_dim

        \# Attention bottleneck over X\_i^c (or X\_i) \-\> reduced to match X\_i dimension (feat\_dim)  
        self.attention \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Conv1d(in\_attn\_dim, attn\_dim, kernel\_size=1, bias=True),  
            nn.Tanh(),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(attn\_dim),  
            nn.Conv1d(attn\_dim, feat\_dim, kernel\_size=1, bias=True)  
        )  
        self.out\_bn \= nn.BatchNorm1d(2 \* feat\_dim)

    def forward(self, x\_i: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        \# x\_i: (B, d\_i, T)  
        if self.use\_ls\_context:  
            ls\_i \= self.ls\_pool(x\_i)                  \# (B, 2\*d\_i, T)  
            x\_ic \= torch.cat(\[x\_i, ls\_i\], dim=1)      \# (B, 3\*d\_i, T)  
        else:  
            x\_ic \= x\_i                                \# (B, d\_i, T)

        alpha \= F.softmax(self.attention(x\_ic), dim=2)  \# (B, d\_i, T)

        \# Attended 1st-order (mean) and 2nd-order (std) statistics over x\_i  
        mean \= torch.sum(alpha \* x\_i, dim=2)          \# (B, d\_i)  
        sq\_mean \= torch.sum(alpha \* (x\_i \* x\_i), dim=2)  
        var \= torch.clamp(sq\_mean \- mean \* mean, min=self.eps)  
        std \= torch.sqrt(var)                         \# (B, d\_i)

        pooled \= torch.cat(\[mean, std\], dim=1)        \# (B, 2\*d\_i)  
        return self.out\_bn(pooled)

class SKAHNN(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Complete SKA-HNN Backbone supporting all Table II configurations (S0/S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6).  
    Paper Full Scale: C=128, C1=512, attn\_dim=256 (30.91M params)  
    Student Scaled Default: C=32, C1=256, attn\_dim=128 (\~2.65M params)  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(  
        self,  
        n\_mels: int \= 80,  
        c\_cnn: int \= 32,  
        c\_tdnn: int \= 256,  
        emb\_dim: int \= 192,  
        attn\_dim: int \= 128,  
        ls\_window: int \= 21,  
        use\_cnn\_frontend: bool \= True,   \# False for S6  
        use\_ska: bool \= True,            \# False for S5  
        use\_mlfc: bool \= True,           \# False for S3, S4  
        use\_ls\_context: bool \= True      \# False for S2, S4  
    ):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.use\_cnn\_frontend \= use\_cnn\_frontend  
        self.use\_mlfc \= use\_mlfc

        if use\_cnn\_frontend:  
            self.conv2d\_in \= nn.Sequential(  
                nn.Conv2d(1, c\_cnn, kernel\_size=3, stride=(2, 1), padding=1, bias=False),  
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),  
                nn.BatchNorm2d(c\_cnn)  
            )  
            self.resblock1 \= SKAResBlock(c\_cnn, freq\_bins=n\_mels // 2, use\_ska=use\_ska)  
            self.resblock2 \= SKAResBlock(c\_cnn, freq\_bins=n\_mels // 2, use\_ska=use\_ska)  
            self.conv2d\_out \= nn.Sequential(  
                nn.Conv2d(c\_cnn, c\_cnn, kernel\_size=3, stride=(2, 1), padding=1, bias=False),  
                nn.ReLU(inplace=True),  
                nn.BatchNorm2d(c\_cnn)  
            )  
            self.d\_c \= c\_cnn \* (n\_mels // 4\)  
        else:  
            \# S6: No 2D-CNN front-end; acoustic features feed directly to TDNN-LSTM  
            self.d\_c \= n\_mels

        self.ls\_c \= LocalStatsPool1d(window\_size=ls\_window)  
        self.tdnn\_lstm \= TDNNLSTMModule(in\_dim=3 \* self.d\_c, out\_dim=c\_tdnn)

        self.ls\_l \= LocalStatsPool1d(window\_size=ls\_window)  
        self.fully\_tdnn \= FullyTDNNModule(in\_dim=3 \* c\_tdnn, out\_dim=c\_tdnn)

        if not use\_mlfc:  
            \# S3 & S4: X\_i \= X\_t only  
            self.d\_i \= c\_tdnn  
        elif not use\_cnn\_frontend:  
            \# S6: X\_i \= \[X\_l; X\_t\]  
            self.d\_i \= 2 \* c\_tdnn  
        else:  
            \# S0, S1, S2, S5: X\_i \= \[X\_c; X\_l; X\_t\]  
            self.d\_i \= self.d\_c \+ 2 \* c\_tdnn

        self.mlasp \= MLASP(  
            feat\_dim=self.d\_i,  
            attn\_dim=attn\_dim,  
            use\_ls\_context=use\_ls\_context,  
            window\_size=ls\_window  
        )

        \# Classification network: Two FC+BN layers projecting 2\*d\_i \-\> 192 \-\> 192  
        self.fc1 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.Linear(2 \* self.d\_i, emb\_dim, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(emb\_dim)  
        )  
        self.fc2 \= nn.Sequential(  
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),  
            nn.Linear(emb\_dim, emb\_dim, bias=False),  
            nn.BatchNorm1d(emb\_dim)  
        )

    def forward(self, mfb: torch.Tensor, extract\_first\_fc: bool \= False) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        \# mfb: (B, F=80, T)  
        B, F\_bins, T \= mfb.shape  
        if self.use\_cnn\_frontend:  
            x \= mfb.unsqueeze(1)                      \# (B, 1, 80, T)  
            x \= self.conv2d\_in(x)                     \# (B, C, 40, T)  
            x \= self.resblock1(x)                     \# (B, C, 40, T)  
            x \= self.resblock2(x)                     \# (B, C, 40, T)  
            x \= self.conv2d\_out(x)                    \# (B, C, 20, T)  
            x\_c \= x.reshape(B, self.d\_c, T)           \# (B, C\*20, T)  
        else:  
            x\_c \= mfb                                 \# (B, 80, T)

        x\_c\_aug \= torch.cat(\[x\_c, self.ls\_c(x\_c)\], dim=1)  \# (B, 3\*d\_c, T)  
        x\_l \= self.tdnn\_lstm(x\_c\_aug)                      \# (B, C1, T)

        x\_l\_aug \= torch.cat(\[x\_l, self.ls\_l(x\_l)\], dim=1)  \# (B, 3\*C1, T)  
        x\_t \= self.fully\_tdnn(x\_l\_aug)                     \# (B, C1, T)

        if not self.use\_mlfc:  
            x\_i \= x\_t  
        elif not self.use\_cnn\_frontend:  
            x\_i \= torch.cat(\[x\_l, x\_t\], dim=1)  
        else:  
            x\_i \= torch.cat(\[x\_c, x\_l, x\_t\], dim=1)        \# (B, d\_i, T)

        utt\_vec \= self.mlasp(x\_i)                          \# (B, 2\*d\_i)  
        emb1 \= self.fc1(utt\_vec)                           \# (B, 192\)  
        if extract\_first\_fc:  
            return emb1  
        emb2 \= self.fc2(emb1)                              \# (B, 192\)  
        return emb2

#### **5.3.3 PyTorch Code: IAAMSoftmax with AdaptiveDrop Label Correction and Filtering (Write Yourself)**

Python  
import math

class IAAMSoftmax(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Improved Additive Angular Margin Softmax (IAAMSoftmax) integrating  
    ArcFace (s=30, m=0.2) with AdaptiveDrop online label correction and filtering.  
    Algorithm 1 in Alam, Fathan, & Alam (IJCNN 2025).  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(  
        self,  
        emb\_dim: int \= 192,  
        num\_classes: int \= 251,  
        scale: float \= 30.0,  
        margin: float \= 0.2,  
        use\_adaptive\_drop: bool \= True,  
        tau: float \= 0.423,         \# cos(65 deg) \= 0.4226  
        tau\_corr: float \= 0.50,     \# High-confidence threshold for label correction  
        esd: int \= 5,               \# Epoch to start dropping noisy samples  
        esc: int \= 7,               \# Epoch to start correcting noisy labels  
        min\_keep\_ratio: float \= 0.25 \# Safeguard against empty batch collapse  
    ):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.emb\_dim \= emb\_dim  
        self.num\_classes \= num\_classes  
        self.scale \= scale  
        self.use\_adaptive\_drop \= use\_adaptive\_drop  
        self.tau \= tau  
        self.tau\_corr \= tau\_corr  
        self.esd \= esd  
        self.esc \= esc  
        self.min\_keep\_ratio \= min\_keep\_ratio

        self.weight \= nn.Parameter(torch.FloatTensor(num\_classes, emb\_dim))  
        nn.init.xavier\_uniform\_(self.weight)

        self.update\_margin(margin)

    def update\_margin(self, margin: float):  
        self.margin \= margin  
        self.cos\_m \= math.cos(margin)  
        self.sin\_m \= math.sin(margin)  
        self.th \= math.cos(math.pi \- margin)  
        self.mm \= math.sin(math.pi \- margin) \* margin

    def forward(self, embeddings: torch.Tensor, labels: torch.Tensor, current\_epoch: int \= 1):  
        """  
        embeddings: (B, emb\_dim)  
        labels: (B,) integer class indices in \[0, num\_classes \- 1\]  
        current\_epoch: 1-indexed epoch counter  
        Returns: (loss, stats\_dict)  
        """  
        \# 1\. L2-normalize sample embeddings omega and class centers omega\_c  
        norm\_emb \= F.normalize(embeddings, p=2, dim=1)          \# (B, D)  
        norm\_weight \= F.normalize(self.weight, p=2, dim=1)      \# (C, D)

        \# 2\. Compute cosine similarities CS(x, c) for all c in {0, ..., C-1}  
        cosine \= F.linear(norm\_emb, norm\_weight).clamp(-1.0 \+ 1e-7, 1.0 \- 1e-7)  \# (B, C)

        rectified\_labels \= labels.clone()  
        num\_corrected \= 0  
        B \= labels.size(0)

        \# 3\. Stage 1: AdaptiveDrop Label Correction (if epoch \> ESC)  
        if self.training and self.use\_adaptive\_drop and current\_epoch \> self.esc:  
            with torch.no\_grad():  
                cs\_assigned \= cosine.gather(1, rectified\_labels.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)  
                max\_cs, best\_class \= cosine.max(dim=1)  
                \# Correct suspicious labels that fall below tau on assigned class but exceed tau\_corr on another class  
                needs\_correction \= (cs\_assigned \< self.tau) & (max\_cs \>= self.tau\_corr)  
                rectified\_labels \= torch.where(needs\_correction, best\_class, rectified\_labels)  
                num\_corrected \= int(needs\_correction.sum().item())

        \# 4\. Stage 2: AdaptiveDrop Sample Filtering (if epoch \> ESD)  
        if self.training and self.use\_adaptive\_drop and current\_epoch \> self.esd:  
            with torch.no\_grad():  
                cs\_target \= cosine.gather(1, rectified\_labels.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)  
                keep\_mask \= cs\_target \>= self.tau

                \# Safeguard: retain at least min\_keep\_ratio of batch with highest CS to prevent NaN/collapse  
                min\_keep \= max(int(B \* self.min\_keep\_ratio), 2\)  
                if int(keep\_mask.sum().item()) \< min\_keep:  
                    topk\_idx \= torch.topk(cs\_target, k=min\_keep, largest=True).indices  
                    keep\_mask \= torch.zeros\_like(keep\_mask, dtype=torch.bool)  
                    keep\_mask\[topk\_idx\] \= True  
        else:  
            keep\_mask \= torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool, device=embeddings.device)

        cosine\_clean \= cosine\[keep\_mask\]  
        labels\_clean \= rectified\_labels\[keep\_mask\]

        \# 5\. Compute AAMSoftmax (ArcFace) over filtered clean batch  
        sine \= torch.sqrt((1.0 \- torch.pow(cosine\_clean, 2)).clamp(1e-7, 1.0))  
        phi \= cosine\_clean \* self.cos\_m \- sine \* self.sin\_m  
        phi \= torch.where(cosine\_clean \> self.th, phi, cosine\_clean \- self.mm)

        \# Construct one-hot mask for ground-truth class y\_i (fixing Eq. 3 j \!= y\_i index)  
        one\_hot \= torch.zeros\_like(cosine\_clean)  
        one\_hot.scatter\_(1, labels\_clean.view(-1, 1).long(), 1.0)

        logits \= (one\_hot \* phi) \+ ((1.0 \- one\_hot) \* cosine\_clean)  
        logits \= logits \* self.scale

        loss \= F.cross\_entropy(logits, labels\_clean)

        stats \= {  
            "keep\_ratio": float(keep\_mask.float().mean().item()),  
            "num\_corrected": num\_corrected,  
            "mean\_target\_cs": float(cosine.gather(1, rectified\_labels.unsqueeze(1)).mean().item())  
        }  
        return loss, stats

#### **5.3.4 PyTorch / NumPy Code: Trial-List Builder and Exact EER / minDCF Evaluator**

Python  
import random  
from pathlib import Path  
from collections import defaultdict  
import numpy as np  
from scipy.optimize import brentq  
from scipy.interpolate import interp1d  
from sklearn.metrics import roc\_curve

def build\_librispeech\_trials(  
    manifest\_rows: list,  
    output\_path: str,  
    num\_target: int \= 15000,  
    num\_impostor: int \= 15000,  
    seed: int \= 42  
):  
    """  
    manifest\_rows: list of dicts with keys {'utt\_id', 'spk\_id', 'chapter\_id', 'gender', 'rel\_path', 'duration'}  
    Builds cross-chapter target trials and gender-matched impostor trials.  
    """  
    rng \= random.Random(seed)  
    spk\_to\_utts \= defaultdict(list)  
    gender\_to\_spks \= defaultdict(list)

    for row in manifest\_rows:  
        if float(row\["duration"\]) \>= 2.0:  \# Filter out ultra-short \<2.0s fragments  
            spk\_to\_utts\[row\["spk\_id"\]\].append(row)

    for spk\_id, utts in spk\_to\_utts.items():  
        gender\_to\_spks\[utts\[0\].get("gender", "U")\].append(spk\_id)

    speakers \= list(spk\_to\_utts.keys())  
    trials \= set()  
    target\_list, impostor\_list \= \[\], \[\]

    \# 1\. Generate Target Trials (prioritize cross-chapter pairs)  
    attempts \= 0  
    while len(target\_list) \< num\_target and attempts \< num\_target \* 20:  
        attempts \+= 1  
        spk \= rng.choice(speakers)  
        utts \= spk\_to\_utts\[spk\]  
        if len(utts) \< 2:  
            continue  
        u1, u2 \= rng.sample(utts, 2\)  
        \# Enforce different chapter\_id if speaker has multiple chapters  
        chapters \= {u\["chapter\_id"\] for u in utts}  
        if len(chapters) \> 1 and u1\["chapter\_id"\] \== u2\["chapter\_id"\]:  
            continue  
        pair\_key \= tuple(sorted(\[u1\["rel\_path"\], u2\["rel\_path"\]\]))  
        if pair\_key not in trials:  
            trials.add(pair\_key)  
            target\_list.append(f"1 {pair\_key\[0\]} {pair\_key\[1\]}")

    \# 2\. Generate Impostor Trials (prioritize same-gender impostors)  
    attempts \= 0  
    while len(impostor\_list) \< num\_impostor and attempts \< num\_impostor \* 20:  
        attempts \+= 1  
        gender\_pool \= rng.choice(list(gender\_to\_spks.values()))  
        if len(gender\_pool) \>= 2:  
            s1, s2 \= rng.sample(gender\_pool, 2\)  
        else:  
            s1, s2 \= rng.sample(speakers, 2\)  
        u1 \= rng.choice(spk\_to\_utts\[s1\])  
        u2 \= rng.choice(spk\_to\_utts\[s2\])  
        pair\_key \= tuple(sorted(\[u1\["rel\_path"\], u2\["rel\_path"\]\]))  
        if pair\_key not in trials:  
            trials.add(pair\_key)  
            impostor\_list.append(f"0 {pair\_key\[0\]} {pair\_key\[1\]}")

    Path(output\_path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist\_ok=True)  
    with open(output\_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:  
        for line in target\_list \+ impostor\_list:  
            f.write(line \+ "\\n")

def compute\_eer\_and\_mindcf(  
    scores: np.ndarray,  
    labels: np.ndarray,  
    p\_target: float \= 0.01,  
    c\_miss: float \= 1.0,  
    c\_fa: float \= 1.0  
):  
    """  
    Computes Equal Error Rate (EER %) and NIST SRE minimum Detection Cost Function (minDCF).  
    """  
    fpr, tpr, thresholds \= roc\_curve(labels, scores, pos\_label=1)  
    fnr \= 1.0 \- tpr

    \# EER via Brent's root-finding method where FNR \== FPR  
    eer \= brentq(lambda x: 1.0 \- x \- interp1d(fpr, tpr)(x), 0.0, 1.0)  
    eer\_threshold \= float(interp1d(fpr, thresholds)(eer))

    \# NIST 2016 SRE minDCF calculation  
    c\_det \= c\_miss \* fnr \* p\_target \+ c\_fa \* fpr \* (1.0 \- p\_target)  
    min\_idx \= int(np.argmin(c\_det))  
    min\_c\_det \= float(c\_det\[min\_idx\])  
    dcf\_threshold \= float(thresholds\[min\_idx\])

    c\_def \= min(c\_miss \* p\_target, c\_fa \* (1.0 \- p\_target))  
    min\_dcf \= min\_c\_det / c\_def

    return {  
        "eer\_percent": float(eer \* 100.0),  
        "eer\_threshold": eer\_threshold,  
        "min\_dcf": float(min\_dcf),  
        "dcf\_threshold": dcf\_threshold,  
        "fpr": fpr,  
        "fnr": fnr  
    }

### **5.4 Side-by-Side Hyperparameter Comparison (Paper Original vs. Student Scaled Default)**

| Hyperparameter | Paper Original Value \[Paper Fact\] | Student Scaled Default \[Engineering Recommendation\] | Engineering Justification for Scaled Choice |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Acoustic Input (![][image50])** | **![][image351]** (25 ms win, 10 ms hop)1 | ![][image351] (25 ms win, 10 ms hop) | Preserves exact time-frequency resolution (![][image352] segments) and frequency downsampling ratios (![][image353]). |
| **2D-CNN Channels (![][image354])** | **![][image158]** (![][image355])1 | ![][image356] (![][image357]) *(Runner-up: ![][image356])* | Reduces 2D-CNN activation memory by ![][image358] and TDNN-LSTM input width from ![][image359] to ![][image360], preventing OOM and overfitting on 251 speakers. |
| **SKA Branches & Kernels** | **![][image361]** branches (![][image40], ![][image41]), ![][image246]1 | ![][image39] branches (![][image40] at ![][image362]), ![][image246] | Exact structural match to Mun et al. (SKA-TDNN)9 and Alam et al.1. |
| **TDNN-LSTM / Fully-TDNN (![][image255])** | **![][image159]** (![][image363])1 | ![][image159] (![][image363]) | Keeps cascade expressive while reducing LSTM and TDNN parameters by ![][image358]. |
| **Combined MLFC Dim (![][image87])** | **![][image1]**1 | ![][image364] | Preserves the exact multi-level concatenation structure ![][image365] at ![][image366] width. |
| **MLASP Context Dim (![][image367])** | **![][image2]** (![][image368])1 | ![][image369] (![][image211]) | Reduces MLASP parameter footprint from ![][image370] to ![][image371]. |
| **Total Backbone Parameters** | **30.91 Million**1 | **2.65 Million** *(or 6.84M at ![][image356])* | Ideal capacity for 28,539 training utterances (train-clean-100); trains in \~55s/epoch. |
| **Embedding Dimension** | **![][image372]**1 | ![][image372] | Kept identical to the paper for direct cosine scoring compatibility1. |
| **Batch Size (![][image373])** | **![][image374]** speakers/utterances1 | ![][image374] utterances (speaker-balanced) | Exact match to the paper1; uses \~3.8 GB VRAM in fp16. |
| **Optimizer & Weight Decay** | Adam1 | AdamW (![][image375], wd=2e-5) | Decoupled weight decay prevents norm explosion before ![][image129]\-normalization. |
| **LR Schedule** | Initial LR ![][image266], triangular cyclic1 | CyclicLR(base\_lr=1e-7, max\_lr=1e-3, mode='triangular2') | Reconciles the paper's stated ![][image266] initial LR with standard triangular cyclic training1. |
| **Training Epochs** | Not stated (typically 40–80 on Vox2)1 | **30 epochs** (Tier 1), **20 epochs** (Tier 2 ablations) | Sufficient for convergence on 100 hours of speech (\~13,400 gradient steps at 30 epochs). |
| **AAMSoftmax ![][image376]** | **![][image377]**, ![][image4]1 | ![][image377], ![][image378] (linear ramp epochs 1–5) | Ramping ![][image379] from ![][image380] to ![][image381] during the 5-epoch warm-up stabilizes prototype alignment before AdaptiveDrop activates. |
| **AdaptiveDrop ![][image382]** | **![][image5]** (![][image6]), ESD \= 5, ESC \= 71 | ![][image5], ESD \= 5, ESC \= 7, min\_keep \= 0.25 | Exact match to the paper and companion ENLSP/ICASSP publications1, plus a 25% minimum batch retention guard. |

## **6\. Tech Stack, Packages, and Skills**

### **6.1 Recommended Software Stack and Hardware-Specific Notes**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** The software stack is selected for deterministic, high-throughput execution across both **Google Colab (Linux x86\_64, CUDA 12.x, NVIDIA T4)** and **Apple MacBook Pro M3 Pro (macOS Sonoma/Sequoia, ARM64 Apple Silicon, MPS backend)**. We recommend native **PyTorch \+ Torchaudio** with selective **SpeechBrain** utilities as the primary framework (**Runner-up**: **WeSpeaker** or **NVIDIA NeMo**, which are heavier to customize for internal fwSKA and AdaptiveDrop hooks).

On Mac M3 Pro, use device="mps"; note that nn.LSTM on mps had backward-pass slowdowns in PyTorch \<2.2, so torch\>=2.3.0 is mandatory. |

(ICASSP 2018\) *X-Vectors: Robust DNN Embeddings for Speaker Recognition* (https\://www\.danielpovey.com/files/2018\_icassp\_xvectors.pdf)1 | **2.5 hrs** |
| **3\. ECAPA-TDNN & Channel-Dependent ASP** | Squeeze-and-Excitation, multi-layer feature aggregation, channel-dependent attentive statistics pooling | Desplanques et al. (Interspeech 2020\) *ECAPA-TDNN* (https\://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07143)1 | **3.0 hrs** |
| **4\. Selective Kernel Attention (SKNet & SKA-TDNN)** | Split-Fuse-Select dynamic receptive fields, fwSKA vs. cwSKA | Li et al. (CVPR 2019\) *Selective Kernel Networks* (https\://arxiv.org/abs/1903.06586)10 & Mun et al. (SLT 2022\) *SKA-TDNN* (https\://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01005)9 | **3.0 hrs** |
| **5\. Angular Margin Losses & AdaptiveDrop** | Hyperspherical projection, ArcFace (![][image384]), noisy label memorization, online correction & filtering | Deng et al. Biometric Metrics (EER, minDCF, DET)** | False Acceptance Rate (FAR), False Rejection Rate (FRR), ROC vs. DET normal deviate scale, NIST SRE cost function | Kaldi compute\_min\_dcf.py documentation (https\://github.com/kaldi-asr/kaldi/blob/master/egs/sre08/v1/sid/compute\_min\_dcf.py)19 | **1.5 hrs** |

## **7\. Training, Evaluation, and Demo Design**

### **7.1 Training Recipe and Collapse Prevention Protocol**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** Training angular-margin hybrid networks with online sample dropping requires careful coordination of data sampling, numerical precision, and margin warm-up. In Dataset.\_\_getitem\_\_, each FLAC file is loaded via soundfile.read at 16 kHz to extract a fixed 180-frame segment (![][image385] samples ![][image342])1; longer utterances are uniformly random-cropped, while shorter utterances undergo wrap-around padding. Because Section IV-A specifies that each training batch of 64 consists of 64 randomly selected speakers1, the data loader employs a custom SpeakerBalancedBatchSampler that draws 64 distinct speakers per mini-batch without replacement until all 251 speakers in train-clean-100 have been visited.  
To prevent recurrent gradient spikes across the TDNN-LSTM hybrid layer when using torch.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.float16), gradients are clipped via torch.nn.utils.clip\_grad\_norm\_(model.parameters(), max\_norm=3.0) prior to each AdamW step. Most importantly, applying a full angular penalty of ![][image4] from the very first iteration—when randomly initialized embeddings ![][image127] and class prototypes ![][image386] are nearly orthogonal in ![][image387] (![][image388])—can cause either angular margin collapse or premature sample rejection once AdaptiveDrop activates at Epoch 6 (epoch \> ESD \= 5\)1. To eliminate this failure mode, the trainer linearly ramps the margin ![][image379] from ![][image380] at Epoch 1 to ![][image381] at Epoch 5 (loss\_fn.update\_margin(0.2 \* min(1.0, (epoch \- 1\) / 4.0))) and continuously monitors two health telemetry signals in TensorBoard: mean\_target\_cs (which must exceed ![][image389] by the end of Epoch 5\) and keep\_ratio (guarded by min\_keep\_ratio \= 0.25 in IAAMSoftmax.forward so that at least 16 samples per batch of 64 are always retained even under 40% synthetic label noise).

### **7.2 Evaluation Protocol, Confidence Intervals, and Cross-Condition Tests**

**\[External Source & Engineering Recommendation\]** Evaluation follows the official NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluation (SRE) and SpeechBrain / Kaldi VoxCeleb conventions17. The primary threshold-free metric is the **Equal Error Rate (EER %)**, defined at the threshold ![][image289] where False Acceptance Rate equals False Rejection Rate: ![][image390]18. The primary calibrated cost metric is the **Minimum Detection Cost Function (minDCF)**, evaluated at prior target probability ![][image391], miss cost ![][image392], and false-alarm cost ![][image393] (https\://speechbrain.readthedocs.io/en/latest/API/speechbrain.utils.metric\_stats.html)17:  
![][image394]  
Because ![][image395], this normalizes to ![][image396]19, heavily penalizing false acceptances in high-security authentication scenarios. To prove to examiners that differences between SKA-HNN (![][image21]) and baselines/ablations are statistically significant, the evaluation script resamples the 30,000 trial pairs with replacement ![][image397] times (stratified by target/impostor label) and reports 95% confidence intervals (![][image398]). Beyond full-duration testing on test-clean (Condition 1\) and test-other (Condition 2), the evaluation suite runs a **Short-Utterance Robustness Study (Condition 3\)**—truncating test utterances in test-clean to ![][image399], ![][image400], and ![][image401] versus **Full Duration** to demonstrate how multi-scale fwSKA/cwSKA and local statistics pooling preserve accuracy on brief speech segments9—and an **Additive Noise Degradation Study (Condition 4\)** at ![][image402].

During the **5-Minute Examiner Walkthrough**, spend **Minute 0:00–1:00** on Tab 5 framing the paper's three contributions (fwSKA/cwSKA 2D-CNN, MLASP with local statistics, and IAAMSoftmax with AdaptiveDrop)1. Spend **Minute 1:00–2:30** on Tab 1 recording a 4-second live enrollment phrase followed by a completely different spoken sentence (or a sentence in a second language to showcase text- and language-independence1), demonstrating a cosine similarity ![][image412] and a green **VERIFIED** decision. Spend **Minute 2:30–3:30** on Tab 2 inviting an examiner to speak into the microphone against the enrolled voiceprint, showing the cosine score dropping into the red impostor distribution (![][image413]) and triggering **REJECTED**. Spend **Minute 3:30–5:00** on Tab 3 and Tab 5 showing how MLASP frame attention ignores leading/trailing silence, how fwSKA shifts weight between ![][image40] and ![][image41] kernels across formant bands, and how IAAMSoftmax prevents label-noise memorization in Tier 3\. In case of browser microphone permission issues or classroom acoustic interference during the viva, selecting any of the six pre-packaged WAV scenarios in app/demo\_assets/ via the Tab 1 fallback dropdown executes the entire verification and visualization pipeline offline with one click.

### **7.5 Reproducibility Checklist**

**\[Engineering Recommendation\]** To guarantee deterministic, auditable results across all experiments, src/utils/seed.py seeds Python's random, numpy.random, torch.manual\_seed(42), and torch.cuda.manual\_seed\_all(42) while setting torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic \= True. All generated trial lists (trials\_dev\_clean.txt, trials\_test\_clean.txt, trials\_test\_other\_hard.txt) are hashed via SHA-256 in data/manifests/checksums.sha256 so that every baseline and ablation is scored on the exact same 30,000 utterance pairs. Finally, every training run automatically writes its resolved OmegaConf YAML configuration, git commit hash, and pip freeze environment lockfile into checkpoints/\<exp\_name\>/.
